_commit: `_commit {operation_id}` applies an approved operation in three transactions: it claims one durable attempt (state running, written and committed before any business side effect), applies the business transaction (approval consumption, writes, readback, receipt, audit; the receipt carries the claimed attempt id) and then records the attempt's outcome in its own transaction, so a rolled-back attempt still leaves history. A repeat returns the same stored receipt as already_applied and queues nothing; without approval it fails with approval_required, after expiry or a write-epoch rotation (`connector_owner_switches`) with expired_intent. That includes an operation whose reviewed source changed before the owner switched the connector back on: the caller it is bound to gets expired_intent, matching _status; any other connection or person gets the opaque denied.

Denied with a reason: _commit and _status agree for the operation's owner. For an unexpired operation that cannot commit (its reviewed source or disclosure version changed, a role a command reads through ${{ user.role }} changed, or its approval no longer holds: the approving session ended, or auto-approve or the tool's consent went away), _status reports state `denied` with `reason` source_changed, actor_changed or approval_lapsed and retryable false, and _commit fails `denied` with the same value in `_meta.reason` and in its text; `reason` is null otherwise. `business` stays as it was (undetermined while an earlier attempt's outcome is unknown, since a block does not settle it). It follows live state, so it clears if the role or source returns. Expiry comes first in both. Any other caller, including another connection of the same person, gets the bare `denied` with no reason.

_status: it reports one of prepared, approved, running, succeeded, failed, conflict, unknown, expired or denied: the receipt wins (succeeded); then expiry; then denied, when _commit would refuse the owner; then the latest attempt (running; unknown; failed; conflict); then approval. It also returns the latest attempt (attempt_id, state, error_class, started_at, finished_at), `retryable`, the business commit (business: committed, not_committed, or undetermined while running or unknown; receipt) and, independently, downstream effects (effects: {status, items}, see `connector_hooks_effects`). A running attempt older than the 30 s coordinator deadline plus a 5 s grace, or one marked succeeded without a receipt, reads as unknown: the business transaction refuses to start once its own claim is stale and cannot COMMIT later than 30 s after the claim.

Conflict and failure: conflict means a dependency set or revision changed since prepare; any other refusal or rollback is failed with its error class (for example hook_refused). A valid apply `expect_rows` mismatch returns `conflict` and records a retryable conflict attempt after rollback; invalid assertions, SQL failures and unavailable row counts are `unavailable_provider`. Infrastructure failures are logged with tool, operation-id prefix and class, return unavailable_provider and are never reported as denied.

Retries: a failed or conflict operation may be committed again while it is unexpired and approved, except a constraint_failed or invalid_declaration failure (at most 5 attempts per operation, then operation_limit; a conflict stays a conflict until the dependencies match again, otherwise prepare anew); a concurrent attempt is refused with in_progress. _status says whether another attempt may follow (retryable): true after failed or conflict and for an unknown whose claim went stale without a receipt, false for an unknown COMMIT outcome.

Unknown outcomes: an unknown COMMIT outcome is reconciled, never replayed: _commit reads the durable receipt (present means succeeded and the operation is never applied again), and without one it stays unknown (_commit fails unknown_execution) until the operation expires. A stale claim with no receipt is superseded: the next _commit marks it unknown (audited, error class stale_claim) and claims afresh in the same transaction, which also covers a crash after the claim or a failed outcome record. The outcome record waits for the write lock on its own 35 s budget (it serializes with key rotation) and is tried up to 3 times. A new claim's started_at is never earlier than its predecessor's, so a clock that steps back cannot wedge an operation; the apply step refuses once fewer than a second remains before its commit deadline.

Who may commit: an operation is usable only by the connector grant that prepared it. Commit also requires the approving browser session to still exist, be unexpired and remain a direct unscoped login, so logging out or narrowing it kills its approval. A receipt replay skips the reviewed-source digest check and _status only reports its result; both verify the actor, account incarnation, workspace and grant, and they work only while the loaded generation, revision enrollment and command declaration are current. Turning writes off hides the tools and 404s the review routes; re-enabling rotates the write epoch, so earlier operations never run.

Limits: each actor may hold at most 20 live unexpired unfinished operations (further prepares fail with operation_limit); unfinished operations and their approvals are deleted one hour after expiry, up to 100 per prepare, while receipts are kept.

Audit: prepare, approve and commit each write an audit row carrying the prepared digest. Every failed, conflict or unknown attempt writes an _benmore_audit_log row (mcp_command_attempt_failed, _conflict, _unknown) outside the rolled-back transaction, with only the attempt id and class.
